extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate public / readers of The Spectator (urban men and women interested in morals, manners, and fashion)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, didactic periodical essays (Spectator‑style) that give social, moral, and aesthetic judgments about everyday behaviour, fashion, and customs for a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lengthen life by pursuing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hours of a wise Man are lengthened by his Ideas; extend Life beyond its natural Dimensions by applying ourselves diligently to the Pursuits of Knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples: employ thoughts on many subjects or a rapid succession of ideas to make time seem longer; contrasted with fools whose passions shorten their time. Invocation of philosophical authorities (Locke, Malebranche) and oriental fables (Mahomet's Night Journey) to illustrate subjective duration. Practical implication for conduct: cultivate knowledge and continuous thought to 'lengthen' one's life experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray subjective time via succession of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our notion of Time is produced by reflecting on the succession of ideas in our mind; accelerating or retarding that succession changes perception of duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this psychological principle when describing mental states: scenes of intense, single-focused thought should compress perceived time; scenes with a fast succession of ideas should expand it. Cited authorities (Locke, Malebranche) and illustrative tales (Mahomet, Turkish tale of the Sultan) provide narrative models for representing altered time perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: True affliction is inward and not theatrical
rubrics_metrics.description: True Affliction labours to be invisible, is a Stranger to Ceremony, and bears a Dignity much above the little Circumstances affected under the Notion of Decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of social practice: condemns judging sorrow by external signs (weeping, gestures). Advises writers (and readers) to recognize that outward demonstrations (tears, shrugs) are superficial; deep grief may be tearless and silent. Examples and anti-patterns: 'impertinent Waiter' who reads facial muscles as prognostics; caution against fashionable, performative mourning. Suggested rhetorical stance: defend inward sincerity and ridicule affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not evaluate grief solely by outward signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Weeping and external demonstrations are fallacious measures of sorrow; people commonly weep without deep sorrow and suffer deeply without tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting or judging mourning, avoid conflating visible tears with moral depth. Offer corrective advice to 'shallow Critics and Observers' who measure affection by handkerchiefs and facial contortions. Use natural-history analogies (children's transient tears) to illustrate inconstancy of external signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female instruction: improve within one's sphere and cultivate virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should be improved in their own sphere — be better Daughters, Wives, Mothers, and Friends — rather than merely aspire to be scholars like men; a little philosophy can help subdue passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance advocacy for reading with caution: recommend practical studies (arithmetick) and moderate philosophy to govern passions. Endorse Fenelon's 'Education of a Daughter' as suitable guidance; dispute the idea that only great ladies can use such instruction. List virtues to cultivate: justice, gratitude, sincerity, prudence, modesty. Anti-pattern: pursuing learning as mere competitive display rather than moral/domestic improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge servants in context of masters' example
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants are not inherently rogues; their behaviour mirrors the example set by their superiors and the conditions (board-wages, living away from the family) under which they are raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative evidence (Thomas Trusty's life) shows servants may be men of wit and sense; bad habits arise from system defects (wages, lack of domestic upbringing). Practical implication: evaluate servants with attention to structural causes and the influence of masters, and beware of sweeping moral judgments. Anti-pattern: blaming servants alone without examining masters' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outlaw duels; prize forgiveness and public order
rubrics_metrics.description: Duels invert the rules of good society and honour; forgiveness of injuries should be esteemed and duelling punished severely to stop the fashion of private combats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral rationale: duels make forgiveness vile and valorise vice; social effects include suppression of virtue and encouragement of wanton courage. Legal prescriptions (Pharamond's Edict): ban challengers/acceptors from public office, seize personal estates of participants, vest real estate in heirs, apply death plus forfeiture when appeal for blood succeeds, and prohibit royal pardons. Use as model for strongly-worded prescriptive prose combining moral argument with concrete legislative penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in fashion: avoid extravagant head-dress
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to add ornament to Nature's masterpiece (the head); excessive head-dress destroys the symmetry of the human figure and diverts the eye from real beauty to childish gewgaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (the Fontange, medieval conical head-dresses) and the monk Thomas Conecte's moral campaign illustrate the excess and social reaction. Practical advice to female readers: prefer natural symmetry, eschew towering superstructures of ribbons, lace, and wire. Recommend using times when fashion favours modesty to suppress extravagance; anti-patterns include constructing 'Gothick' piles that mock natural proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public example and law to curb fashionable excess
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reign (or favorable public fashion) is the proper time to attack exorbitance; public censure and laws (or social pressure) can effectively check extravagant fashions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate with the success of preachers and public ridicule (bonfires of head-dresses) in suppressing an extravagant mode; advise writers/policymakers to act when public sentiment is amenable. Use satire and moral persuasion to prevent recurrence (compare to women who 'shot out their horns' again after the danger passed).
